pool.q: A 64-year-old white woman presents with complaints of pain, decreased vision, and a red eye for the past 2 days (Fig. 8-1). Her medical history reveals that she had a trabeculectomy for primary open-angle glaucoma in this same eye 6 months before. What would a Gram stain of the vitreous fluid of this patient most likely show?
pool.rationale: Gram-negative coccobacilli This patient has filtering bleb–associated endophthalmitis. The most common organisms responsible for this condition include Streptococcus species (gram-positive cocci in pairs or chains) and Haemophilus influenzae (gram-negative coccobacilli). Other organisms, such as S. epidermidis (gram-positive cocci in clusters) and gram-negative species, have been implicated less frequently. Fungal causes are rarely associated with filtering bleb–associated endophthalmitis. The organisms are thought to enter the eye through either intact or leaking conjunctival filtering blebs. Often, Seidel testing is negative. Common presenting symptoms include conjunctival discharge and injection, pain, and decreased vision. The prognosis for eyes with bleb-associated endophthalmitis is generally poor, and the end result is often phthisis.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q1

pool.q: A 69-year-old white man presents with mild discomfort and reports a gradual decrease in the vision of his right eye over the course of 1 week. His ocular history is remarkable for cataract extraction and posterior chamber intraocular lens (IOL) insertion in this eye 4 months previously. Because of the low-grade nature of the inflammation, topical steroids are begun, and the inflammation responded favorably. After discontinuing the steroids, the symptoms return and the patient again presents with a granulomatous anterior chamber inflammation, including a small hypopyon and a mild anterior vitritis. What would examination of the white plaque present at the equator of the posterior lens capsule most likely reveal?
pool.rationale: Propionibacterium acnes This patient’s condition is suspicious for chronic postoperative endophthalmitis. Organisms commonly responsible for delayed-onset endophthalmitis after cataract surgery include S. epidermidis, fungal species such as Candida, and P. acnes. Endophthalmitis caused by P. acnes typically presents from 3 months to 2 years after surgery, whereas S. epidermidis generally presents within 6 weeks and Candida within 3 months. The presence of a white plaque within the capsular bag specifically suggests the diagnosis of P. acnes. Microscopic examination of plaques removed at the time of vitrectomy has revealed P. acnes.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q2

pool.q: A 69-year-old white man presents with mild discomfort and reports a gradual decrease in the vision of his right eye over the course of 1 week. His ocular history is remarkable for cataract extraction and posterior chamber intraocular lens (IOL) insertion in this eye 4 months previously. Because of the low-grade nature of the inflammation, topical steroids are begun, and the inflammation responded favorably. After discontinuing the steroids, the symptoms return and the patient again presents with a granulomatous anterior chamber inflammation, including a small hypopyon and a mild anterior vitritis. Which one of the following is the most appropriate therapy for this condition?

options.a: Vitrectomy and intravitreal injection of amphotericin B
options.c: Vitrectomy, removal of the IOL, and intravitreal injection of gentamicin
options.d: Vitrectomy, posterior capsulectomy, and intravitreal injection of vancomycin

pool.rationale: Vitrectomy, posterior capsulectomy, and intravitreal injection of vancomycin The clinical picture suggests delayed-onset postoperative endophthalmitis caused by P. acnes. This condition often responds initially to topical steroids; however, inflammation will recur. Although simple intravitreal injection of vancomycin has resulted in clearing of this infection, recurrences are common. Currently, recommendations for initial therapy include a pars plana vitrectomy with posterior capsulectomy and intravitreal injection of vancomycin. An alternative advocated by some surgeons is a posterior pole vitrectomy, IOL explant, posterior capsulectomy, intravitreal vancomycin, and a sutured IOL. Recurrence rates for intravitreal antibiotic injection, vitrectomy with intravitreal antibiotics, vitrectomy with partial capsulectomy and intravitreal antibiotics, and vitrectomy with total capsulectomy combined with IOL removal or exchange and intravitreal antibiotics are 83%, 50%, 26%, and 0%, respectively.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q3

pool.q: A 69-year-old white man presents with mild discomfort and reports a gradual decrease in the vision of his right eye over the course of 1 week. His ocular history is remarkable for cataract extraction and posterior chamber intraocular lens (IOL) insertion in this eye 4 months previously. Because of the low-grade nature of the inflammation, topical steroids are begun, and the inflammation responded favorably. After discontinuing the steroids, the symptoms return and the patient again presents with a granulomatous anterior chamber inflammation, including a small hypopyon and a mild anterior vitritis. What is the least likely microbial cause for this syndrome?
pool.rationale: Klebsiella In addition to the more common organisms responsible for delayed-onset postoperative endophthalmitis such as P. acnes, S. epidermidis, and Candida, other organisms, including P. granulosum, Achromobacter, and Corynebacterium, have been reported to cause this syndrome. Klebsiella or other gram-negative bacilli may be seen in endogenous endophthalmitis but would be an unlikely cause of delayed-onset postoperative endophthalmitis.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q4

pool.q: A 32-year-old African American woman presents with floaters and blurred vision in her right eye. Slit lamp examination shows nodules on the iris (Fig. 8-2). A recent chest radiograph revealed hilar adenopathy. Biopsy of her lacrimal gland would likely reveal:

options.b: multinucleated giant cells of the Touton type
options.c: multinucleated giant cells of the Langhans type

pool.rationale: Multinucleated giant cells of the Langhans type The clinical description of a chronic diffuse uveitis with evidence of a choroidal granuloma and hilar adenopathy is highly suggestive of sarcoidosis. A lacrimal gland biopsy is useful in the diagnosis of sarcoidosis, especially if it is enlarged at the time of the biopsy. The gland is involved in approximately 25% of patients. The histologic lesion found in sarcoid biopsies is the noncaseating epithelioid cell tubercle. The tubercle is composed of multinucleated giant cells of the Langhans type surrounded by a rim of lymphocytes. Touton giant cells classically are found in juvenile xanthogranuloma.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q5

pool.q: A 32-year-old African American woman presents with floaters and blurred vision in her right eye. Slit lamp examination shows nodules on the iris (Fig. 8-2). A recent chest radiograph revealed hilar adenopathy. Other ocular manifestations include all of the following except:
pool.rationale: Follicular conjunctivitis Sarcoid has many protean manifestations affecting almost all of the ocular structures. Inflammation and granulomas may be found as conjunctival nodules, infiltration of the lacrimal gland, anterior uveitis with Koeppe and Busacca nodules, vitreitis, chorioretinal nodules, papillitis, and scleritis. The sequelae of chronic inflammation include keratoconjunctivitis sicca, band keratopathy, synechiae, and glaucoma. Follicular conjunctivitis is commonly found in viral conjunctival infections.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q6

pool.q: A 32-year-old African American woman presents with floaters and blurred vision in her right eye. Slit lamp examination shows nodules on the iris (Fig. 8-2). A recent chest radiograph revealed hilar adenopathy. Ocular complications in this condition as a result of steroid treatment include all of the following except:
pool.rationale: Retinal neovascularization Treatment of sarcoid uveitis often requires topical, sub-Tenon, or systemic corticosteroid therapy. Many ocular and systemic complications may occur as a result of this medication. Ocular complications include cataract formation, steroidinduced glaucoma, scleral thinning, and delayed wound healing. Neovascularization of the retina may occur with sarcoid, but this is a result of inflammation and ischemia, not a consequence of steroid therapy.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q7

pool.q: An 11-year-old white girl presents with reports of floaters in her left eye and a mild decrease in vision. On examination of her anterior chamber, you notice a mild anterior chamber inflammatory reaction and the corneal changes shown in Figure 8-3. Dilated fundus examination reveals whitish fibrous material in the inferior periphery. Which one of the following is associated with this condition?

options.c: Unilaterality in the majority of cases

pool.rationale: Multiple sclerosis This presentation of band keratopathy, a mild anterior chamber reaction, vitreous cells, and a pars plana “snowbank” in a young patient, is highly suggestive of the diagnosis of pars planitis. Multiple sclerosis has been associated with this condition in approximately 5% of cases, and the condition is bilateral approximately 80% of the time. Other associated findings include posterior subcapsular cataracts, anterior chamber synechiae, macular epiretinal membranes, retinal phlebitis, and cystoid macular edema.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q8

pool.q: An 11-year-old white girl presents with reports of floaters in her left eye and a mild decrease in vision. On examination of her anterior chamber, you notice a mild anterior chamber inflammatory reaction and the corneal changes shown in Figure 8-3. Dilated fundus examination reveals whitish fibrous material in the inferior periphery. Pathologic examination of the “snowbank” would reveal:

options.c: an aggregation of epithelioid and multinucleated giant cells
options.d: a conglomeration of lipofuscin and chronic inflammatory cells

pool.rationale: Fibroglial and vascular components Histologically, the snowbank is composed of fibroglial and vascular elements. It is not an exudate, but a preretinal membrane that forms in response to an inflammatory stimulus. The membrane also contains vascular elements that occasionally bleed and result in a vitreous hemorrhage. The peripheral retinal veins often show a perivascular cuff of lymphocytes, and the vitreous snowballs are composed of epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q9

pool.q: A patient presents with the eye illustrated in Figure 8-4. All of the following conditions can cause this except:
pool.rationale: Uveitis–glaucoma–hyphema (UGH) syndrome This patient has a severe anterior uveitis with a hyphema. Any severe uveitis can cause damage to the iris vasculature, resulting in anterior chamber bleeding. In particular, VZV iridocyclitis and HLA-B27 (see Fig. 8-4) can result in this picture. A traumatic injury can cause a tear at the iris root in addition to inciting an anterior uveitis. Dispersed blood and fibrin can appear similar to active uveitis. The UGH syndrome is the result of movement of an anterior chamber IOL, which chafes the iris and angle, causing inflammation and bleeding. This patient is phakic; therefore, this etiology is not possible.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q10

pool.q: Which one of the following conditions is not typically associated with diffusely distributed keratic precipitates?
pool.rationale: Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome The following conditions may be associated with diffusely distributed keratic precipitates over the corneal endothelium: Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis, sarcoidosis, syphilis, kerato uveitis, and, rarely, toxoplasmosis. Most inflammatory conditions, including Vogt–Koyanagi– Harada syndrome, display keratic precipitates predominantly over the inferior portion of the corneal endothelium. The finding of diffusely distributed keratic precipitates may be a useful diagnostic sign.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q11

pool.q: Which one of the following conditions is not associated with HLA-B27–linked acute iritis?
pool.rationale: Behçet disease The HLA-B27 genotype is present in approximately 1% to 6% of the general population; however, it may be found in a larger percentage of patients with acute iritis. HLA-B27 is found in almost 90% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis. It also is commonly associated with conditions such as psoriatic arthritis, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, and reactive arthritis. Patients with Behçet disease, however, have an increased incidence of HLA-B5 or subset Bw51.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q12

pool.q: A 35-year-old man presents with ocular pain, pain in his wrists and feet, pain on urination, and aphthous ulcers. Ocular examination is significant because it reveals a mucoid conjunctival discharge and a mild cellular reaction in the anterior chamber. A peculiar skin lesion is also noted (Fig. 8-5). Which one of the following findings would not be expected in this patient?
pool.rationale: Positive rheumatoid factor The triad of urethritis, conjunctivitis, and arthritis has described classic reactive arthritis. Other associations include keratoderma blennorrhagicum; iritis, keratitis, balanitis, prostatitis, cystitis, spondylitis, fasciitis, tendonitis, oral mucosal lesions, and a recent history of diarrhea. HLA-B27 genotype is present in approximately 75% of cases. Rheumatoid factor is usually not present.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q13

pool.q: A 35-year-old man presents with ocular pain, pain in his wrists and feet, pain on urination, and aphthous ulcers. Ocular examination is significant because it reveals a mucoid conjunctival discharge and a mild cellular reaction in the anterior chamber. A peculiar skin lesion is also noted (Fig. 8-5). Which organism has not been implicated in triggering this condition?
pool.rationale: Rochalimaea Reactive arthritis may occur after dysentery or after nongonococcal urethritis. Ureaplasma urealyticum and Chlamydia trachomatis have been associated with the postgenitourinary form. Shigella, Salmonella, and Yersinia have also been shown to be triggers for this condition after episodes of diarrhea or dysentery caused by these agents. Rochalimaea has been implicated as causing cat-scratch fever and neuroretinitis but not this condition.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q14

pool.q: A 35-year-old man presents with ocular pain, pain in his wrists and feet, pain on urination, and aphthous ulcers. Ocular examination is significant because it reveals a mucoid conjunctival discharge and a mild cellular reaction in the anterior chamber. A peculiar skin lesion is also noted (Fig. 8-5). The classic skin lesion associated with this condition, pictured in Figure 8-5, is:
pool.rationale: Keratoderma blennorrhagicum Skin involvement may be seen in reactive arthritis in approximately 20% of cases. The classic lesion is known as keratoderma blennorrhagicum and is pictured in Figure 8-5. When present, this condition is considered a major criterion in making the diagnosis of Reactive arthritis. The other major criteria include polyarthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis. Minor criteria are signs, such as fasciitis, sacroiliitis, spondylitis, keratitis, cystitis, prostatitis, oral mucosal lesions, and diarrhea. Definite diagnosis of reactive arthritis is defined by three or more major criteria, or two major criteria and two minor criteria.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q15

pool.q: A 10-year-old girl with a history of arthralgia and a chronic anterior chamber inflammation of both eyes presents to your office. She has no cells, but mild flare is present in the anterior chamber. Given the natural history of this disease, which one of the following statements is most likely true?

options.b: This patient has pauciarticular disease involving the hands and wrists.
options.c: This patient has pauciarticular disease involving the lower extremities without involvement of the wrist joints.

pool.rationale: This patient has pauciarticular disease involving the lower extremities without involvement of the wrist joints. JRA presents in children younger than 16 years of age. Approximately 80% of patients with JRA and iritis are ANA positive and rheumatoid factor–negative. The joint involvement in JRA may be polyarticular or pauciarticular (four or fewer joints). When iridocyclitis is present, the joint involvement is most commonly of the pauciarticular type (90% of cases). Systemic JRA with fever and rash is rarely associated with iritis. ANA–positive females with pauciarticular involvement of a lower extremity joint and lack of involvement of the wrists are at highest risk for developing iritis. The anterior chamber inflammation in chronic JRA is characterized by a mild variable degree of anterior chamber cellular reaction with predominance of flare. The conjunctiva is generally quiet.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q16

pool.q: A 40-year-old white man is referred for ophthalmologic examination because the vision in one eye could not be refracted better than 20/40. On examination, you note a mild unilateral anterior chamber inflammation and stellate keratic precipitates diffusely dispersed over the posterior surface of the cornea. The patient has hazel irides with a mild difference of iris pigmentation between the eyes. Which one of the following statements is most likely true?

options.a: The involved eye is darker brown than the uninvolved eye.
options.b: Less than 2% of patients with this condition will have bilateral involvement with no obvious heterochromia.
options.c: Pathologic specimens of this condition have revealed the presence of plasma cells within the ciliary body.

pool.rationale: Pathologic specimens of this condition have revealed the presence of plasma cells within the ciliary body. This patient has Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis. This condition is generally characterized by heterochromia, although up to 15% of cases may have bilateral involvement without obvious heterochromia. Diffuse iris stromal atrophy with variable pigment epithelial layer atrophy accounts for the change in iris color in the involved eye. Because of the pigment loss, brown eyes will appear less brown; blue eyes will appear more blue. This condition is also characterized by small, white, stellate keratic precipitates that are diffusely present over the endothelial surface. Synechiae are almost never present. The inflammatory nature of this disease is supported by the presence of plasma cells and lymphocytes on pathologic examination of ocular tissue.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q17

pool.q: A 40-year-old white man is referred for ophthalmologic examination because the vision in one eye could not be refracted better than 20/40. On examination, you note a mild unilateral anterior chamber inflammation and stellate keratic precipitates diffusely dispersed over the posterior surface of the cornea. The patient has hazel irides with a mild difference of iris pigmentation between the eyes. Which one of the following infectious agents has been suggested as having an association with this condition?
pool.rationale: Toxoplasma This condition is clearly associated with chorioretinal scars consistent with toxoplasmosis; however, whether Toxoplasma is a causative agent is unclear. Not all cases of Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis have chorioretinal scars. Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is a syndrome, rather than a distinct entity, which has also been associated with rubella virus and appears to be decreasing in incidence possibly due to MMR vaccination.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q18

pool.q: A 40-year-old white man is referred for ophthalmologic examination because the vision in one eye could not be refracted better than 20/40. On examination, you note a mild unilateral anterior chamber inflammation and stellate keratic precipitates diffusely dispersed over the posterior surface of the cornea. The patient has hazel irides with a mild difference of iris pigmentation between the eyes. Which of the following topical medications used unilaterally can cause a similar appearance?
pool.rationale: Latanoprost The prostaglandin analogues have several proinflammatory side effects, including inciting development of an anterior uveitis and a cystoid macular edema. Unilateral use can also result in changes in iris pigmentation and eyelash growth. The anterior uveitis resolves with topical prednisolone and discontinuation of the causative drug.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q19

pool.q: All of the following major immunoglobulin classes are found in human tears except:
pool.rationale: IgD IgD has not been detected in any study of human tears. The major immunoglobulin class found in human tears is IgA. IgG and IgM are detectable in only small amounts. IgE is thought to be one of the major mediators of allergic reactions. In contrast, all five immunoglobulins are found routinely in the human conjunctiva within the subepithelial tissue.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q20

pool.q: Which one of the following statements concerning the classic immune hypersensitivity reactions in diseases that affect the eye is true?

options.a: The granulomatous response seen in sarcoid uveitis is primarily a type I hypersensitivity reaction.
options.b: Phacoanaphylaxis is a type III hypersensitivity reaction.
options.c: Hay fever is an example of a type II hypersensitivity reaction.
options.d: Type IV hypersensitivity reactions are mediated by cytotoxic antibodies.

pool.rationale: Phacoanaphylaxis is a type III hypersensitivity reaction. There are four general types of hypersensitivity reactions. One of the four types will predominate in any inflammatory response, although several types may be involved at the same time. Type I inflammatory responses are antibody mediated. The binding of antibody to mast cells releases histamine, leukotrienes, and other inflammatory mediators. Allergic reactions, such as hay fever, are type I reactions. Type II reactions are mediated by cytotoxic antibodies such as those seen with ocular pemphigoid. Type III reactions are immune complex–mediated. Antibody binds with free-floating or fixed antigens and then deposits as a complex, activating the complement cascade. Phacoanaphylaxis fits into this category. Finally, type IV reactions are T cell–mediated reactions. The granulomatous responses seen in sarcoid or tuberculosis are examples of type IV reactions.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q21

pool.q: An elderly African American patient comes with the complaint of a whitish area on her eye for the last several weeks (Fig. 8-7). Her eye has been comfortable. There is no discharge or crusting of the lashes. All of the following blood tests would be useful in making the diagnosis except:
pool.rationale: HIV antibodies
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q22

pool.q: An elderly African American patient comes with the complaint of a whitish area on her eye for the last several weeks (Fig. 8-7). Her eye has been comfortable. There is no discharge or crusting of the lashes. There is a small trickle of fluid from the peripheral corneal defect. What treatment might be most helpful in the acute setting?
pool.rationale: Application of cyanoacrylate glue This patient has severe rheumatoid arthritis with peripheral ulcerative keratitis. The hands of this patient (Fig. 8-31) show the stereotypic deformities from rheumatoid arthritis. Other conditions to consider include other collagen vascular diseases (ANCA-associated vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa, relapsing polychondritis), Mooren ulcer, and infections such as tuberculosis and syphilis. Peripheral ulcerative keratitis is not a hallmark of HIV infection or AIDS. Rheumatoid patients can have spontaneous painless corneal melting. In the acute phase, topical steroids are contraindicated because they can potentiate the corneal collagenases and increase the melting. These patients can be glued temporarily until systemic prednisone and immunosuppressive agents are started. Grafts in an inflamed eye are at high risk for failure or recurrent melting.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q23

pool.q: Which one of the following characteristics regarding serpiginous choroidopathy is true?
pool.rationale: Recurrent, indolent course Serpiginous choroidopathy (geographic helicoid peripapillary choroidopathy) is a chronic, recurrent, indolent disease of unknown etiology. It usually affects adults with painless loss of vision. Lesions are peripapillary or perimacular and, in the active phase, have inflammation along the edges. Centrifugal spread in a snake-like pattern occurs over months to years. Treatment with steroids or immunosuppressive agents has had variable success. Tuberculosis must be excluded prior to initiation of anti-inflammatory therapy.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q24

pool.q: A 25-year-old man was hammering a nail into a piece of wood in his garage when he noticed a sudden sharp pain in his right eye with only a mild decrease in his vision. He presents to your office 2 days later with reports of gradually increasing pain and a severe loss of vision in that eye. On examination, you notice a small peripheral corneal laceration and a hypopyon. Which one of the following statements concerning endophthalmitis in this setting is true?

options.a: The most common infecting organism in these cases is Staphylococcus aureus.
options.b: A visual acuity of 20/400 or better is likely to be retained in the majority of patients after appropriate treatment and rehabilitation.
options.c: Endophthalmitis would be expected to occur in less than 10% of similar trauma cases.
options.d: Endophthalmitis with Bacillus species has a good visual prognosis.

pool.rationale: Endophthalmitis would be expected to occur in less than 10% of similar trauma cases. Posttraumatic endophthalmitis after penetrating trauma typically occurs in fewer than 10% of cases. The most common agents responsible for this infection include S. epidermidis and Bacillus species, although many other organisms have been recovered. The prognosis for visual recovery in this setting is generally poor, especially when Bacillus cereus is implicated.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q25

pool.q: You examine a 78-year-old white man with complaints of decreased vision in his right eye. Three weeks earlier, he had undergone coronary artery bypass surgery with a complicated postoperative course requiring prolonged ventilatory support. He has been receiving hyperalimentation and IV antibiotics since the time of his surgery. On dilated fundus examination of his right eye, you note a fluffy white choroidal lesion under the macula. There is minimal overlying vitritis present. Which one of the following statements concerning the organism most likely responsible for this lesion is true?

options.a: The responsible organism grows on blood agar and Sabouraud glucose within 24 to 48 hours.
options.b: This organism exists exclusively as an oval budding cell known as a blastoconidia.
options.c: Ocular infection caused by this organism is generally accompanied by positive blood cultures.
options.d: This organism often colonizes the respiratory tract and is a frequent cause of pneumonia.

pool.rationale: The responsible organism grows on blood agar and Sabouraud glucose within 24 to 48 hours. This fundus lesion in the setting of a debilitated patient on hyperalimentation and previous antibiotics is highly suggestive of endogenous endophthalmitis often caused by Candida albicans. Most cases of Candida endophthalmitis occur without ongoing fungemia or positive blood cultures. All Candida species exist in two morphologic forms: a yeastlike form known as blastoconidia (pseudohypha) and elongated branching structures (pseudomycelia). Candida species typically grow on blood agar and Sabouraud glucose within 24 to 48 hours. They grow as large creamy-white colonies. A germ tube test from a colony of only 24 hours’ duration can result in a presumptive diagnosis of C. albicans. Although this organism is frequently cultured from the respiratory tract, it rarely causes pneumonia.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q26

pool.q: A 25-year-old homeless man presents to your office with reports of decreased vision and pain in his right eye for the past 2 days. Examination reveals marked conjunctival injection, a 2-mm hypopyon, and dense vitreous opacities on B-scan ultrasound. You suspect endogenous endophthalmitis, and on further questioning, the patient admits to IV drug abuse. Given the patient’s history, which one of the following organisms is the least likely to be involved in this patient’s endophthalmitis?
pool.rationale: Haemophilus influenzae Endophthalmitis as a complication of IV drug abuse has been widely reported. The most common organisms in these cases are fungal in origin and often occur in the absence of fungemia. Bacterial causes are predominantly a result of Staphylococcus species; however, recently B. cereus has been reported as an important pathogen. Although H. influenzae can cause infection, it would be unusual in this setting.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q27

pool.q: A 27-year-old Japanese exchange student presents to your office with reports of decreased vision in both his eyes. On examination, a small hypopyon OD and a moderate cellular reaction OS is found. Fundus examination of his left eye is shown in Figure 8-8. On further questioning, you elicit a history of arthritis of his knees and wrists, and painful lesions in his mouth and around his genitals. On examination of his lower extremities, you note the lesion seen in Figure 89. Skin lesions common to this condition include all of the following except:

options.a: acne-like lesions over the back and face

pool.rationale: Psoriasis Patients with Behçet disease frequently have a variety of associated skin lesions. Lesions resembling erythema nodosum are frequently present over the anterior surface of the lower extremities. These lesions typically resolve over a period of several weeks. Patients may also display typical acne-like lesions, folliculitis, or thrombophlebitis. Cutaneous hypersensitivity is also characteristic of this condition. The behçetine (pathergy) skin test performed by puncturing the skin with an empty hypodermic needle may be useful in making a diagnosis of Behçet disease. A positive test is indicated by the formation of a pustule at the puncture site within minutes. The pathergy test is most likely to yield a positive result in Mediterranean individuals, less likely to be positive in Middle Eastern countries and Japan, and least likely to be positive in the United States.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q28

pool.q: A 27-year-old Japanese exchange student presents to your office with reports of decreased vision in both his eyes. On examination, a small hypopyon OD and a moderate cellular reaction OS is found. Fundus examination of his left eye is shown in Figure 8-8. On further questioning, you elicit a history of arthritis of his knees and wrists, and painful lesions in his mouth and around his genitals. On examination of his lower extremities, you note the lesion seen in Figure 89. Which one of the following statements concerning the therapeutic treatment of this condition is true?

options.a: Oral corticosteroids alone are usually effective in preventing the relapse of ocular inflammation.
options.b: Periocular steroids alone are usually effective in preventing the relapse of ocular inflammation.
options.c: Colchicine may be helpful in preventing recurrences.
options.d: Cyclosporine may be useful in this condition, but the incidence of liver toxicity may limit its use.

pool.rationale: Colchicine may be helpful in preventing recurrences. Commonly used agents in the treatment of Behçet disease include systemic corticosteroids, cytotoxic agents (alkylating agents such as chlorambucil), colchicine, and cyclosporine. Systemic corticosteroids may be initially effective in treating the ocular inflammation in this condition; however, its use has clearly not been found to arrest the long-term progress of this condition. Colchicine is known to inhibit leukocyte migration and has been found to be useful in preventing recurrences. Cyclosporine has also been found to be particularly useful in the treatment of Behçet disease; however, its use must be carefully monitored because of renal toxicity.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q29

pool.q: A 27-year-old Japanese exchange student presents to your office with reports of decreased vision in both his eyes. On examination, a small hypopyon OD and a moderate cellular reaction OS is found. Fundus examination of his left eye is shown in Figure 8-8. On further questioning, you elicit a history of arthritis of his knees and wrists, and painful lesions in his mouth and around his genitals. On examination of his lower extremities, you note the lesion seen in Figure 89. Which one of the following statements concerning the ocular inflammation associated with this condition is true?

options.a: Patients generally develop chronic, unremitting ocular inflammation if this condition is not aggressively treated.
options.b: A granulomatous inflammation is typically present.
options.c: The retinitis associated with this condition may be confused with a viral retinitis.
options.d: Inflammation in this condition predominantly affects the choroid.

pool.rationale: The retinitis associated with this condition may be confused with a viral retinitis. Inflammation in Behçet disease may affect the anterior and posterior segments and is generally a bilateral process. Recurrent explosive inflammatory episodes are typical with active episodes that range from 2 to 4 weeks. A chronic, lingering inflammatory stage typically does not develop. A nongranulomatous anterior uveitis with formation of a transient hypopyon is common. Posterior inflammation is characterized by recurrent vascular occlusive episodes with retinal hemorrhage and vitreous inflammation. The inflammation is typically confined to the retina and retinal vasculature. Choroidal involvement is rarely seen. The retinitis of Behçet disease is very suggestive of a viral retinitis and must be considered in the differential.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q30

pool.q: What is the most common cause of acute, noninfectious, hypopyon iritis?
pool.rationale: HLA-B27–associated iritis The most common cause of hypopyon iritis is HLA-B27–associated disease. Hypopyon is present in 10% to 30% of cases of Behçet uveitis.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q31

pool.q: In which one of the following is the HLA-B27 antigen least likely to be present?

options.b: Young women with pauciarticular juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA)

pool.rationale: Young women with pauciarticular juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA) Young women with early-onset pauciarticular disease commonly have antinuclear antibodies. The rheumatoid factor is not present in this group. Patients with late-onset pauciarticular disease are predominantly men and have a high incidence of HLA-B27–associated iridocyclitis. The rheumatoid factor–positive polyarticular disease and the rheumatoid factor–negative polyarticular disease are rarely, if ever, associated with uveitis.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q32

pool.q: Which form of uveitis is most common in ocular sarcoidosis?
pool.rationale: Anterior uveitis Two-thirds of patients with sarcoid uveitis have anterior uveitis. Two forms of anterior uveitis exist. One is a chronic, recurrent anterior uveitis that is difficult to treat and control with corticosteroids. The other is an acute granulomatous iridocyclitis that responds well to corticosteroid therapy.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q33

pool.q: Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding the lesions pictured in Figure 810?

options.a: Live virus can be recovered from epithelial lesions.
options.b: This disease is usually seen in children or young adults.
options.c: Topical corticosteroid drops are effective in eliminating this disease.
options.d: These lesions are frequently bilateral at presentation.

pool.rationale: Live virus can be recovered from epithelial lesions. Varicella zoster epithelial keratitis is depicted. Differences between herpes simplex keratitis are outlined here. An accompanying vesicular eruption is frequently present (Fig. 8-32) (Table 8-1). Acute Varicella Zoster Herpes simplex dendrites pseudodendrites Active viral Yes Yes replication Multiple branching, slightly elevated Appearance Branching, ulcerated lesions with terminal bulbs lesions Vesicular eruption in V1 dermatome, Skin rash Vesicular eruption affecting lids resolves with scarring Usually unilateral, can be bilateral in atopic or Laterality Unilateral immunosuppressed patients
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q34

pool.q: Select the answer that corresponds to the conditions listed. Iris nodules
pool.rationale: Granulomatous uveitis
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q35

pool.q: Select the answer that corresponds to the conditions listed. Epithelioid cells
pool.rationale: Granulomatous uveitis Diffusely distributed keratic precipitates may be seen in herpetic iridocyclitis or in Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis. Herpetic iridocyclitis is typically granulomatous. Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is chronic and nongranulomatous. Granulomatous iridocyclitis is often marked by iris nodules and mutton fat keratic precipitates. Histopathologically, the presence of epithelioid cells is pathognomonic for granulomatous inflammation.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q36

pool.q: Select the answer that corresponds to the conditions listed. Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis
pool.rationale: Nongranulomatous uveitis Eyes with Fuchs uveitis classically demonstrate nongranulomatous inflammation with small or fine, stellate keratic precipitates distributed diffusely over the corneal endothelium and fine vessels in the anterior chamber, which may hemorrhage during paracentesis (Amsler sign). If prior intraocular surgery has not ocurred, iris synechiae should not be present. There are rare reports of Fuchs uveitis patients with iris nodules, large and granulomatous-appearing keratic precipitates, and iris synechiae, although these cases are rare and atypical for this syndrome.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q37

pool.q: (Figs. 8-11 to 8-14) Biopsy of which lesion would show a monotonous proliferation of B cells?
pool.rationale: Figure 8-11
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q38

pool.q: (Figs. 8-11 to 8-14) Which would present with pain and localized tenderness?
pool.rationale: Figure 8-10
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q39

pool.q: (Figs. 8-11 to 8-14) Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) has been implicated in causing which condition?
pool.rationale: Figure 8-12 Figure 8-10 is a patient with nodular scleritis. Patients present with a deep aching pain. The inflamed vessels are deep in the sclera and do not blanch with topical phenylephrine. Figure 8-11 shows periocular lymphoma. This pinkish tumor sculpts itself to the scleral surface. These tumors frequently are proliferation of B cells. Excision can be curative. Systemic spread is rare. Figure 8-12 is conjunctival Kaposi sarcoma in a patient with AIDS. This tumor has been associated with HHV-8. No treatment is necessary for ocular lesions unless they are bulky and unsightly. Doxorubicin has been used for systemic treatment. With immune reconstitution, these lesions may regress. Figure 8-13 is a patient with benign conjunctival chemosis due to sensitivity to airborne allergens.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q40

pool.q: What is the most characteristic side effect of oral cyclophosphamide?
pool.rationale: Hemorrhagic cystitis Adequate hydration, which may include either oral intake of 2 to 3 L of fluid or IV infusion of 1 to 2 L of fluid, is important to prevent hemorrhagic cystitis with the use of cyclophosphamide. Hemorrhagic cystitis increases the risk of bladder cancer development. Oral cyclophosphamide is more likely to produce hemorrhagic cystitis than is IV cyclophosphamide. Adjuvant MESNA may reduce the incidence of hemorrhagic cystitis.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q41

pool.q: Side effects of systemic corticosteroid therapy include all of the following except:
pool.rationale: Hypoglycemia Systemic corticosteroid therapy has been associated with numerous complications. Ocular complications include cataracts and glaucoma. Systemic complications include exacerbation of hypertension or diabetes mellitus, osteoporosis, gastric ulceration, hirsutism, weight gain, capillary fragility, and cushingoid appearance.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q42

pool.q: Match the following immunosuppressives to their class. Cyclosporine
pool.rationale: Immune modulator of interleukin 2
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q43

pool.q: Match the following immunosuppressives to their class. Prednisone
pool.rationale: Cytostatic anti-inflammatory
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q44

pool.q: Match the following immunosuppressives to their class. Methotrexate
pool.rationale: Cytotoxic antimetabolite Cyclosporine and FK506, a related agent, are potent immune modulators that have very specific activity against the production of interleukin-2 and interleukin-2 receptors and inhibit proliferation of lymphocytes. Prednisone is a cytostatic anti-inflammatory agent that is a nonspecific immunosuppressive. Cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil are both cytotoxic alkylating agents. They act by creating cross-linkage between DNA strands that result in inhibition of transcription of messenger RNA. Chlorambucil is the slowest acting of all the alkylating agents. Azathioprine and methotrexate both inhibit purine ring biosynthesis. In addition, methotrexate also inhibits the synthesis of deoxythymidine monophosphate nucleotide.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q45

pool.q: Which one of the following is the most common retinal finding in AIDS?
pool.rationale: Cotton wool spots Cotton wool spots may occur in over 50% of AIDS patients. The cotton wool spots may spontaneously resolve and recur. The most common opportunistic infection of the eye is CMV retinitis. Acute retinal necrosis is secondary to herpesvirus retinal infection.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q46

pool.q: The life form of the Toxoplasma gondii organism that is responsible for stimulating inflammation is/are:
pool.rationale: Tachyzoite Toxoplasma organisms tend to be dormant in the cyst form in the intermediate human host. In the encysted form, several dormant organisms may be found. These relatively inactive organisms within the cysts are called bradyzoites. Once bradyzoites are released and become free, they are called tachyzoites. These metabolically energized protozoans are responsible for stimulation of intraocular inflammation.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q47

pool.q: Which one of the following statements about the drugs used to treat ocular toxoplasmosis is true?

options.a: Pyrimethamine blocks the production of dihydrofolate from para-aminobenzoic acid.
options.b: Sulfadiazine inhibits the dihydrofolate reductase enzyme.
options.c: Clindamycin can effectively kill Toxoplasma organisms.
options.d: Systemic and periocular corticosteroids are contraindicated because they may cause proliferation of Toxoplasma organisms.

pool.rationale: Clindamycin can effectively kill Toxoplasma organisms. Pyrimethamine actually inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. Sulfadiazine blocks the production of dihydrofolate from para-aminobenzoic acid. Clindamycin is an antibiotic that can effectively kill Toxoplasma organisms. Systemic and periocular steroids can be used in the treatment of ocular toxoplasmosis in immunocompetent patients.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q48

pool.q: JRA-associated iridocyclitis is most common in:
pool.rationale: Early-onset pauciarticular disease Pauciarticular early-onset JRA is the entity associated most commonly with chronic, recurrent iridocyclitis. It is seen in young women. The ANA is often present in these patients, but rheumatoid factor is uniformly absent. Arthritis of the lower extremities is more common in patients with iridocyclitis.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q49

pool.q: Schwartz syndrome is caused by:

options.a: retinal pigment epithelial cells blocking the trabecular meshwork
options.b: forward rotation of the lens–iris diaphragm
options.d: photoreceptor outer segments blocking the trabecular meshwork

pool.rationale: Photoreceptor outer segments blocking the trabecular meshwork Schwartz syndrome is high IOP associated with a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. Photoreceptor outer segments migrate transvitreally into the aqueous, block the trabecular outflow pathways, and result in IOP elevation.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q50

pool.q: Posner–Schlossman syndrome:

options.a: requires systemic or periocular corticosteroid therapy
options.b: is not associated with late-onset glaucoma

pool.rationale: Is often self-limited Posner–Schlossman syndrome presents with unilateral ocular pain, mild anterior uveitis, and elevated IOP. The episodes that occur are typically self-limited, but they often require the use of topical glaucoma medications to control IOP. Mild topical corticosteroids may be used to control intraocular inflammation. Systemic and periocular corticosteroids are not indicated. Recurrent attacks of this syndrome may lead to eventual optic nerve damage and late-onset glaucoma.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q51

pool.q: Match the following disease entities with the type of inflammation. Phacoanaphylactic endophthalmitis:
pool.rationale: Zonal granulomatous inflammation
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q52

pool.q: Match the following disease entities with the type of inflammation. Phacolytic glaucoma:
pool.rationale: Macrophages filled with lens material Lens-induced uveitis syndromes may produce granulomatous or nongranulomatous inflammation. Although phacoanaphylaxis implies type I hypersensitivity reactions, the word is a misnomer because it represents a type III immune hypersensitivity reaction to lens protein that results in a zonal granulomatous inflammation. Macrophages filled with lens materials often clog the trabecular meshwork and result in phacolytic glaucoma. IOLs may produce phacotoxic nongranulomatous inflammation by physically irritating the iris or ciliary body. The UGH syndrome is a type of phacotoxic uveitis.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q53

pool.q: Which one of the following regarding acute retinal necrosis is not true?

options.b: Herpes zoster virus has been implicated as etiologic agent.
options.c: Posterior pole is involved initially with centrifugal spread.

pool.rationale: Posterior pole is involved initially with centrifugal spread. Acute retinal necrosis was first described in healthy, immunocompetent patients. Herpes simplex and zoster viruses have been implicated as causing this condition. Patients present with vitritis, confluent peripheral necrotizing retinitis, and retinal arteritis with vaso-occlusion. The posterior pole typically is spared until late in the disease. Retinal detachments are common because of the multiple, large areas of retinal necrosis.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q54

pool.q: Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is characterized by:

options.a: high rate of posterior capsular rupture during phacoemulsification
options.c: neovascular proliferation in the angle with angle closure
options.d: resolution of iridocyclitis with topical corticosteroids

pool.rationale: Filiform hemorrhage with paracentesis Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is typically an insidious, chronic intraocular inflammation that may not respond well to topical corticosteroids. Characteristic findings include diffusely distributed stellate keratitis precipitates and mild anterior segment cell and flare with loss of iris crypts and detail. Blue irides become more blue, and brown irides become less brown in cases of Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis. Gonioscopy will reveal evidence of abnormal bridging vessels in the angle, although neovascular glaucoma with angle closure does not develop. A paracentesis of the anterior chamber may result in a small, splinter-shaped filiform hemorrhage in the angle. Fifty percent of patients with Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis develop cataracts; 60% develop glaucoma. Cataract surgery is not associated with any higher rate of vitreous loss or posterior capsular rupture compared to normal eyes.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q55

pool.q: Intermediate uveitis is associated with all of the following conditions except:
pool.rationale: Syphilis Although syphilitic uveitis may mimic any other form of uveitis, intermediate uveitis is a distinctly uncommon presentation. Pars planitis is by far the most common intermediate uveitis entity, a diagnosis of exclusion. Between 5% and 25% of patients with multiple sclerosis may have evidence of periphlebitis and intermediate uveitis.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q56

pool.q: Complications of pars planitis include all of the following except:
pool.rationale: Choroidal neovascularization Calcific band keratopathy can develop in young patients with pars planitis. Peripheral retinal neovascularization can result in vitreous hemorrhage and tractional detachments. Progression of tractional detachments can result in rhegmatogenous components, as well. Choroidal neovascularization is not an associated complication of pars planitis. Cystoid macular edema is the most common macular complication of pars planitis and the most common cause of vision loss. Approximately 10% of eyes with pars planitis will develop cataracts, macular edema, epiretinal membrane, snowbank neovascularization, and retinal detachment. Pars planitis is not a benign entity; forty percent of affected individuals in one cohort suffered blindness or visual impairment when followed over a 15-year period.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q57

pool.q: The electroretinogram in the condition pictured in Figure 8-15: Second Edition. Philadelphia: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2011.
pool.rationale: Reveals diminished scotopic responses Because of the peripheral creamy choroidal infiltrates, retinochoroidopathy, peripheral visual field loss, nyctalopia, and rod dysfunction seen in birdshot retinochoroidopathy, electroretinogram reveals diminished scotopic responses.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q58

pool.q: Cystoid macular edema is a common cause of visual loss in all of the following except:
pool.rationale: Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome Cystoid macular edema is not typically seen in patients with Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome. Patients with this disorder present with bilateral panuveitis and evidence of disc edema and bilateral multiple serous detachments. In chronic cases, pigmentary changes may be present in the fundus, but cystoid macular edema is not. In addition to the entities listed, any iridocyclitis can cause cystoid macular edema, especially chronic, recurrent cases.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q59

pool.q: The strongest HLA association to ocular disease is between:
pool.rationale: HLA-A29 and birdshot retinochoroidopathy The association between HLA-A29 and birdshot retinochoroidopathy is the most consistent of any medical disorder. Approximately 90% of patients with birdshot retinochoroidopathy are HLA-A29–positive (Table 8-2).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q60

pool.q: Which one of the following regarding diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis is true?

options.b: Treatment is mainly with systemic corticosteroids.
options.c: Reduced vision, vitreous cells, and optic disc edema are early findings.

pool.rationale: Reduced vision, vitreous cells, and optic disc edema are early findings. Diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis is thought to be caused by numerous different types of roundworms. Baylisascaris species (raccoon parasites) have been implicated most consistently in northern climates. Ancylostoma species are more common in southern climates. In early phases of the disorder, reduced vision, vitreous cell, and disc edema are common and may mimic a white dot syndrome. As the disorder progresses, eventual optic atrophy, retinal vascular sclerosis, and diffuse pigmentary changes may be seen, resulting in the unilateral wipe-out syndrome. The meticulous evaluation of the fundus for the presence of a small roundworm in the subretinal space, followed by retinal photocoagulation of this worm, can arrest the progression of this disease.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q61

pool.q: Which one of the following statements regarding sarcoidosis is true?

options.a: Elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level is specific for sarcoidosis.
options.b: Blind conjunctival biopsies have a high yield in patients with presumptive diagnosis of sarcoidosis.
options.c: Hilar adenopathy is the most common pulmonary finding in sarcoidosis.
options.d: Uveitis occurs in 85% of patients with systemic sarcoidosis.

pool.rationale: Hilar adenopathy is the most common pulmonary finding in sarcoidosis. Elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme levels may be seen in any diffuse granulomatous disease affecting the lung. Random conjunctival biopsies have a characteristically low yield (25%) in patients who have only the presumptive diagnosis of sarcoidosis. If the diagnosis has been made based on elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme levels and a positive chest radiograph, conjunctival biopsies may have yields as high as 60% to 70% for noncaseating granulomas. Pulmonary findings of sarcoid include no changes, hilar adenopathy, and diffuse interstitial lung disease that may progress to severe end-stage pulmonary fibrosis. Ocular involvement occurs in approximately 25% of patients with systemic sarcoidosis. Uveitis may be seen in up to 60% of patients with ocular involvement.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q62

pool.q: A 65-year-old patient presents with a painful, red eye for the past 3 months. The eye is illustrated in Figure 8-16. Appropriate laboratory evaluation would include:
pool.rationale: Serum anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q63

pool.q: A 65-year-old patient presents with a painful, red eye for the past 3 months. The eye is illustrated in Figure 8-16. Appropriate therapy would include all of the following except:
pool.rationale: Colchicine
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q64

pool.q: A 65-year-old patient presents with a painful, red eye for the past 3 months. The eye is illustrated in Figure 8-16. Which one of the following should never be used to treat this condition?
pool.rationale: Periocular corticosteroids Treatment of scleritis with periocular corticosteroids is controversial and should not be employed in the initial treatment phase. Once a definitive diagnosis is established, infectious conditions have been excluded, no tendency toward necrotizing scleritis has been observed, and a favorable response to topical or systemic corticosteroids has been established, then subconjuctival corticosteroids may be an appropriate alternative.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q65

pool.q: A 65-year-old patient presents with a painful, red eye for the past 3 months. The eye is illustrated in Figure 8-16. All of the following systemic conditions may be associated with Figure 8-16 except:
pool.rationale: Polymyalgia rheumatica Figure 8-15 shows a patient with severe necrotizing scleritis. Patients will present with severe pain, photophobia, and a red eye. Underlying blue uveal tissue may be seen, giving the redness of the scleritis a violaceous hue. Acute therapy should consist of oral prednisone 1 to 2 mg/kg/day with the eventual addition of cytotoxic immunosuppressives. A thorough investigation for associated systemic vasculitides should be completed. Periocular corticosteroids should be avoided because depot steroids may enhance collagenase activity in polymorphonuclear leukocytes and result in further scleral melting and necrosis. There is no role for biopsy of the sclera for diagnostic purposes. Although polymyalgia rheumatica is an inflammatory condition, it does not manifest as scleritis.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q66

pool.q: A patient with the fundus pictured in Figure 8-17 is referred for your evaluation. The work-up of this patient would include:
pool.rationale: Lumbar puncture
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q67

pool.q: A patient with the fundus pictured in Figure 8-17 is referred for your evaluation. Appropriate treatment would include:

options.b: intrathecal methotrexate, IV cytarabine (Ara-C), and whole brain and eye irradiation
options.d: no treatment is available for this condition.

pool.rationale: Intrathecal methotrexate, IV cytarabine (Ara-C), and whole brain and eye irradiation
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q68

pool.q: A patient with the fundus pictured in Figure 8-17 is referred for your evaluation. Which one of the following regarding this condition is true?

options.a: There is poor prognosis for survival.
options.d: Cystoid macular edema is a common complication.

pool.rationale: There is poor prognosis for survival. Figure 8-16 shows the characteristic presentation of primary intraocular lymphoma. This leopard skin pattern of yellowish retinal pigment epithelium and subretinal infiltration of lymphomatous cells are typically seen in patients over the age of 70 years. These patients often present initially with vitritis that may be unilateral or bilateral. The initial laboratory evaluation of the vitritis may be noncontributory. However, evaluation of the CNS with MRI, CT scanning with contrast, and lumbar puncture may reveal evidence of CNS lymphoma. Pars plana vitrectomy may be required to establish diagnosis and to stage the neoplasm. Once the diagnosis has been made and staging has been completed, therapy typically consists of combinations of intrathecal methotrexate, IV cytotoxic agents, and whole brain and ocular irradiation. Periocular and systemic steroids may mask the vitritis and reduce the intraocular inflammation, but inflammation would recur on discontinuation of the medications. The prognosis for survival is dismal in patients who have intraocular lymphoma. Primary intraocular lymphoma is a subset of primary CNS lymphoma. Once symptoms of CNS involvement have occurred, median survival drops to approximately 6 months.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q69

pool.q: This patient has a granulomatous uveitis with multiple serous retinal detachments as shown in Figure 8-18. Work-up should include:
pool.rationale: All of the above
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q70

pool.q: This patient has a granulomatous uveitis with multiple serous retinal detachments as shown in Figure 8-18. The most appropriate treatment for this condition would be:

options.a: pars plana vitrectomy and internal drainage of subretinal fluid
options.c: scleral buckling with external drainage of subretinal fluid

pool.rationale: Corticosteroids
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q71

pool.q: This patient has a granulomatous uveitis with multiple serous retinal detachments as shown in Figure 8-18. Fluorescein angiography would reveal:

options.a: a single “smokestack” of fluorescein leakage into the subretinal space
options.b: multiple pinpoint areas of fluorescein leakage into the subretinal space
options.c: diffuse retinal venous staining and leakage
options.d: well-defined lacy hyperfluorescence with late leakage

pool.rationale: Multiple pinpoint areas of fluorescein leakage into the subretinal space
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q72

pool.q: This patient has a granulomatous uveitis with multiple serous retinal detachments as shown in Figure 8-18. Differential diagnosis may include all of the following except:
pool.rationale: Acute neuroretinitis The patient in Figure 8-17 has Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome. This diagnosis is one of exclusion, and appropriate laboratory evaluation for this entity should be performed. Vogt– Koyanagi–Harada syndrome is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis that causes disc edema and bilateral serous retinal detachments with panuveitis in the acute phases of the disease. It is important to rule out infectious entities, including syphilis and possibly tuberculosis. An antinuclear antibody test may also be done to rule out lupus choroidopathy. B-mode echography may be useful in showing the amount of choroidal infiltration, which is quite profound in the posterior pole. This condition is treated with systemic corticosteroids. Fluorescein angiography characteristically reveals multiple pinpoint areas of hyperfluorescence that gradually leak fluorescein into the subretinal space. Retinal vascular staining is uncommon. Differential diagnosis would include posterior scleritis, sympathetic ophthalmia, hypotony, uveal effusion syndrome, and lupus choroidopathy. Acute neuroretinitis would not present with serous retinal detachments.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q73

pool.q: All of the following cutaneous features may be found in Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome except:
pool.rationale: Eczema Cutaneous manifestations of Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome include alopecia, vitiligo, and poliosis (whitening of the lashes). These manifestations confirm the notion that melanin is the immunogenic agent that results in the intraocular inflammation in this condition. Eczema has been associated with atopy.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q74

pool.q: Refer to Figures 8-19 to 8-24. All of the following may be associated with Figure 8-23 except:
pool.rationale: Cardiac conduction defects
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q75

pool.rationale: Figure 8-19

pool.q: Refer to Figures 8-19 to 8-24. Which one of the following serologic tests is correctly matched to the disorder?

pool.q: Refer to Figures 8-19 to 8-24. Which one of the following therapies is correctly matched to the disorder?

options.c: Figure 8-22 and triple sulfa and pyrimethamine

pool.rationale: Figure 8-18 and colchicine
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q78

pool.q: Refer to Figures 8-19 to 8-24. The disorder characterized by features in Figures 8-19, 8-21, and 8-24 may also demonstrate which one of the following systemic features?
pool.rationale: Pulmonary artery aneurysm
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q79

pool.q: Refer to Figures 8-19 to 8-24. Which one of the following is most appropriate in the work-up of the patient in Figure 8-22?
pool.rationale: All of the above
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q80

pool.q: Refer to Figures 8-19 to 8-24. Cutaneous abnormalities may occur in all of the following disorders except:
pool.rationale: Figure 8-19 disorder Figure 8-18 shows branch retinal vein occlusion in a patient with Behçet disease. Figure 8-20 shows the hypopyon, and Figure 8-21 shows an aphthous ulcer in a patient with Behçet disease. Figure 8-19 shows a patient with serpiginous retinochoroidopathy. Figure 8-21 shows a patient with retinal periphlebitis, which could be compatible with sarcoidosis, Lyme disease, pars planitis, multiple sclerosis–associated intermediate uveitis, and possibly tuberculosis and Eales disease. Figure 8-23 shows acute hypopyon/plastic iritis in a patient who is HLA-B27– positive. Behçet disease may be associated with painful hypopyon iridocyclitis. However, fibrinous anterior segment inflammation is uncommon. The eye can be remarkably quiet in the presence of a hypopyon in Behçet disease, unlike in HLAB27–associated disease, in which pain and photophobia dominate as symptoms. A strong association with HLA-B5 is often present in Behçet disease. Systemic changes include acne, erythema nodosum, aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and interstitial lung changes. A pulmonary artery aneurysm is a pathognomonic chest radiographic finding in a patient with Behçet disease. Treatment is with systemic and periocular corticosteroids. Colchicine may be useful in reducing recurrences of the disease. Cyclosporine and cytotoxic agents may also be required. Serpiginous choroidopathy is a condition of unknown etiology with recurrent, progressive episodes of painless visual loss. Inflammation occurs at the edges of previous lesions with centrifugal spread. Periphlebitis is seen characteristically in sarcoidosis and Eales disease. Eales disease is endemic in India and is often associated with pulmonary tuberculosis. The exact etiology of Eales disease is unknown. Cutaneous changes are seen in Behçet disease, sarcoidosis, and Lyme disease. Sarcoid skin changes include erythema nodosum and subcutaneous nodules or granulomata. Lyme disease is associated with erythema chronicum migrans (Fig. 8-33).
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q81

pool.q: What is the most common posterior segment opportunistic infection in patients with AIDS?
pool.rationale: CMV retinitis Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) has reduced the incidence of CMV retinitis by 80% to 90%.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q82

pool.q: Patients with AIDS and CMV retinitis:

options.a: have CD4 lymphocyte counts of 100 to 500 cells/mm3
options.b: have a mean survival of 6 months
options.c: have CD4 lymphocyte counts of less than 50 cells/mm3
options.d: have ocular pain and photophobia on presentation

pool.rationale: Have CD4 lymphocyte counts of less than 50 cells/mm3 Patients with CMV retinitis and AIDS uniformly have CD4 counts of less than 50. CMV retinitis is by far the most common posterior segment opportunistic infection in patients with AIDS. Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis may be a distant second. Patients with CMV retinitis often present with floaters and peripheral visual field loss. Mean survival after the presentation of CMV retinitis has improved dramatically with the use of appropriate systemic antiviral therapy and HAART therapy.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q83

pool.q: Which one of the following is not true of ocular toxoplasmosis in patients with AIDS?

options.a: Antitoxoplasma IgM antibodies are elevated more often than in immunocompetent patients.
options.b: There are larger areas of retinal necrosis than in immunocompetent patients.
options.c: Vitritis is almost always absent because of lymphopenia.
options.d: Cerebral toxoplasmosis lesions concurrently present in up to 25% of patients.

pool.rationale: Vitritis is almost always absent because of lymphopenia. Ocular toxoplasmosis in AIDS is often associated with significantly more vitreous cells than in CMV retinitis. Although some variability exists as to the amount of vitreous inflammation, based on CD4 counts, vitritis is almost always present to some extent.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q84

pool.q: Which one of the following therapeutic options is appropriate as a first line of therapy for CMV retinitis?

options.a: Induction with 200 µg intravitreal injections of ganciclovir twice weekly
options.b: Induction with 90 to 120 mg/kg IV foscarnet twice daily
options.c: Induction with 5 mg/kg IV ganciclovir twice daily

pool.rationale: All of the above
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q85

pool.q: IV or intravitreal antiviral induction therapy for CMV retinitis is given for:
pool.rationale: 14 days Either IV or intravitreal antiviral therapy may be used for the treatment of CMV retinitis. Oral valganciclovir therapy is equally efficacious compared to intravenous ganciclovir for induction treatment. Induction is typically carried out for 14 days. Once the retinitis is under control, maintenance therapy is given indefinitely.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q86

pool.q: Refer to Figures 8-25 to 8-29. All of these patients have AIDS. Which disorder(s) can be associated with CD4 counts of less than 50 cells/mm3?
pool.rationale: All of the above
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q87

pool.q: Refer to Figures 8-25 to 8-29. All of these patients have AIDS. Elevated intracranial pressure may be found in which one of the following?

pool.q: Refer to Figures 8-25 to 8-29. All of these patients have AIDS. Intravenous ganciclovir is the best therapy for which of the following disorders?
pool.rationale: Figure 8-28

pool.q: Refer to Figures 8-25 to 8-29. All of these patients have AIDS. The anterior segment changes of Figure 8-25 are probably associated with the disorder shown in:
pool.rationale: Figure 8-24

pool.rationale: Figure 8-26

pool.q: Refer to Figures 8-25 to 8-29. All of these patients have AIDS. Retinal detachment may complicate the disorder shown in:
pool.rationale: All of the above Figures 8-24 and 8-25 are from a patient who has AIDS and toxoplasma retinochoroiditis. Figure 8-26 shows a patient who has progressive outer retinal necrosis and who had cutaneous zoster and AIDS on presentation. Figure 8-27 shows a patient who has cryptococcal meningitis and bilateral papilledema. Figure 8-28 shows a patient who has peripapillary CMV retinitis. Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis in patients with AIDS is often marked by intense vitreous inflammation and large areas of retinal necrosis. Treatment consists of triple systemic antitoxoplasma medications. Steroids should be avoided. Up to 25% of patients can have intracranial lesions. Late stages of the disorder may be marked by tractional combined with rhegmatogenous retinal detachments. Mutton fat keratitis precipitates may be dramatic in patients with toxoplasmosis, as is shown in Figure 8-25. Progressive outer retinal necrosis syndrome is a viral retinitis occurring in patients with AIDS who have a previous history of cutaneous zoster. Herpes zoster virus has been implicated in causing this florid outer retinal necrosis. Treatment consists of IV foscarnet, or foscarnet and ganciclovir. The prognosis is poor. The disease becomes bilateral in nearly all cases. Progression is rapid—within a matter of days. The incidence of retinal detachment is approximately 87%. Patients with cryptococcal meningitis present with obstructive hydrocephalus, severe headaches, and very high intracranial pressure. This disease may result in florid papilledema as evidenced in Figure 8-27.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q92

pool.q: Figure 8-30 corresponds to a severely immunosuppressed patient with AIDS. Which of the following treatments is helpful for this condition?
pool.rationale: Pentamidine
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q93

pool.q: Figure 8-30 corresponds to a severely immunosuppressed patient with AIDS. What other organ is commonly involved with this same infection?
pool.rationale: Lungs Figure 8-29 shows the appearance of Pneumocystic carinii infection in an AIDS patient. These patients frequently have CD4 counts of less than 200. Other AIDS-related infections that should be considered include CMV, Cryptococcus, fungi, or other protozoa such as Microsporidia. This protozoan most commonly causes a pneumonitis, but disseminated disease can also result in the yellowish choroidal lesions pictured. Treatment includes trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim), atovaquone, pentamidine, or dapsone.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q94

pool.q: Choroidal neovascularization occurs in which one of the following disorders?
pool.rationale: All of the above Choroidal neovascularization is common in many posterior uveitides. Choroidal inflammation may enhance production of angiogenic factors, and, when coupled with retinal pigment epithelium–Bruch membrane disruption, choroidal neovascularization can develop.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q95

pool.q: The ring-shaped stromal infiltrate seen in herpes simplex keratitis is caused by:
pool.rationale: Antigen–antibody complex precipitation The stromal infiltrate is thought to be similar to the line of precipitation in the Ouchterlony test. Antigens diffuse from one area of the gel, and antibodies diffuse from another. The line forms at the meeting point of the diffusing antigen and antibodies.
pool.ref: Review Questions in Ophthalmology (3rd ed) — Uveitis, Q96
